title: The Mexican martyrs (21 May)
hook: Christopher Magallanes and companions killed during the Cristero years

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernardine of Siena and his board with three letters. Your line was the holy name. Where did you spot IHS? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

¡Viva Cristo Rey! Long live Christ the King. In Mexico, in the years of the Cristero conflict, those words could be a battle cry, a password, a prayer, or the last thing someone said. This week we've met an apostle who asked to see the Father, a replacement chosen by lot, a farmer, a princess of legend, a sailor monk and a preacher with a painted board. Today the week ends in a country where calling Christ king could cost you your life. Today, the Mexican martyrs.
screen: `¡VIVA CRISTO REY!` → `A CRY, A PRAYER, LAST WORDS.` → `THE WEEK ENDS IN MEXICO.`

segments.voice: Some background, kept simple. There was a time when Mexico's government passed harsh laws limiting the Church: priests registered and restricted, schools and orders closed. In protest, the bishops suspended public Masses across the country. Some Catholics took up arms, and the fighters came to be called Cristeros. It was a real war, with violence on more than one side, and the Church doesn't canonize a war. What the Church honors on this day is different. It honors Christopher Magallanes, a parish priest, and a group of companions, priests among them, who were killed for their faith during those years. Tradition remembers Father Magallanes as a pastor who ran a seminary in secret, cared for his people, and did not urge them to take up arms. When he was arrested and brought to be shot, the story goes, he gave away what he had and said he was innocent and forgave those who were about to kill him. Some of the martyrs, tradition says, died with that cry on their lips: Viva Cristo Rey. Here is the line under the whole day. Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." That's the strange part of these martyrs. Their cry sounds like a battle shout. But the ones the Church remembers here are honored for dying without hatred. Long live Christ the King, said by a man forgiving the soldiers in front of him. A king, in this faith, who was crowned with thorns.
screen: `HARSH LAWS, AND A WAR.` · `A PRIEST WHO DIDN'T TAKE UP ARMS.` · `HE FORGAVE HIS KILLERS.` · `A CRY SAID WITHOUT HATRED.` · then, large: `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Mexico. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the country as it is today. Its cities and villages. Its families, its parishes, its priests. People living with violence, and people working for peace. Those who have gone north and those waiting at home. If you pray, you can ask the Mexican martyrs to pray for Mexico, or simply say their cry quietly: long live Christ the King. If you don't, hold the people of Mexico in mind, with goodwill, one face at a time. The bell holds the time.
Christopher Magallanes, the priest remembered with his companions as the Mexican martyrs, killed in the Cristero years, honored for dying without hatred.
Your line: long live christ the king. Today, when someone wrongs you, try answering without hatred, even once. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: On 21 May the Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Christopher Magallanes and companions; in Mexico, Catholics often pray for their country and visit shrines connected to the martyrs.

notes: Claims rule: no years, decades or martyr count spoken. Cristero conflict dates (1926–1929) omitted.
'Priests among them' about the companions: confirm (most were priests, some laymen).
Magallanes running a clandestine seminary, opposing armed rebellion ('by many accounts'), last words of innocence and forgiveness: traditional accounts; confirm.
'The Church doesn't canonize a war': a fair summary? Some Cristero-linked figures have been beatified; check framing.
Politically sensitive: Mexican government laws described as 'harsh laws limiting the Church'; violence acknowledged on more than one side. Confirm balance.
Week end (day 994): hook looks back on days 988–993.
Original is Spanish, not Latin/Greek; keep or set to null.
Editor: hook no longer opens 'Three words', which echoed day 993's 'Three letters'; cut 'by many accounts' (claims rule); 'the Church belonged to Christ' made plainer.

Audit (serious): 'public worship shut down' made the government close the churches; in 1926 it was the Mexican bishops who suspended public worship in protest at the Calles Law. Teach and fork corrected. Magallanes (secret seminary at Totatiche, opposed armed revolt, last words of innocence and forgiveness) and DR Matthew 5:44 checked.
